program_overview.title: Cybersecurity Competitions: picoCTF and CyberPatriot Prep
program_overview.tagline: Two of the best-known student cyber competitions, one defensive skill set, and a clear line between what is allowed and what is not.
program_overview.description:
Student cybersecurity competitions come in two main shapes, and this course prepares for both. CyberPatriot, the National Youth Cyber Education Program created by the Air & Space Forces Association, runs the National Youth Cyber Defense Competition, in which teams of middle and high school students find and fix security vulnerabilities in virtual Windows and Linux systems and are scored on how secure they make them. picoCTF, the capture-the-flag program built at Carnegie Mellon University and now part of CMU's free CyLab Security Academy, sets puzzle challenges in areas such as general skills, cryptography and forensics, each hiding a flag to find.

The first two months build the foundations both need: the Linux command line, Windows administration, how networks move data, and a written white-hat agreement that every student signs before any practice begins. Months three and four are CyberPatriot-style hardening: user and password policy, services, firewalls, updates, permissions and the forensics questions on a practice virtual machine each student sets up with the teacher, worked against the clock and as a team. Months five and six are capture-the-flag skills: encodings and ciphers, file and packet forensics, reading code, and how web and memory bugs are recognised and fixed.

Everything is ethical and defensive. Students practise only on a practice virtual machine they set up with the teacher and on platforms designed for practice, where every challenge is meant to be solved. Nobody is taught to touch a system they do not own or have permission to test, and the legal and ethical lines are taught as part of the skill, not as a disclaimer.
what_makes_this_different: Prepares for both competition styles: CyberPatriot-style defence of Windows and Linux systems, and picoCTF-style capture-the-flag puzzles
Defensive by design: every bug a student finds in a CTF challenge is paired with the fix a defender would make
Practice only on your own practice virtual machine and on purpose-built practice platforms, never on real systems
A white-hat agreement signed in week one and revisited every month, covering permission, disclosure and competition rules
Team skills taught on purpose: roles, checklists and communication during a timed round
Written solutions for every challenge, so students learn to explain their reasoning as well as find the answer

learning_path.phase_2: System hardening in the CyberPatriot style: Windows and Linux hardening checklists, forensics questions, network fundamentals and timed team rounds
learning_path.phase_3: Capture-the-flag skills in the picoCTF style: encodings and cryptography, forensics, reading code, web and memory bugs with their fixes, and a mock CTF

career_outcomes: Confidence on the Linux command line and in Windows security settings
A tested hardening checklist for Windows and Linux systems
A portfolio of written CTF solutions across cryptography, forensics and general skills
A clear understanding of the legal and ethical lines in security work, and the habit of staying on the right side of them

phase_1_foundations_and_ethics.title: PHASE 1: Foundations and Ethics (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_foundations_and_ethics.description: The shared foundations of both competitions, starting with the rules: what is allowed, what is not, and why that line matters.

month_1_ethics_and_linux.title: Month 1: The White-Hat Agreement and the Linux Command Line

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Rules, Ethics and the Practice Lab
topics: Permission as the dividing line between security work and crime
Competition rules: what is allowed during a round and what gets a team disqualified
The white-hat agreement every student signs before practice begins
How CyberPatriot and capture-the-flag events differ, and what each one rewards
Setting up a practice lab with a free virtual machine program
Snapshots: how to break a practice system safely and restore it

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Linux Command Line Essentials
topics: Navigating the file system: pwd, ls, cd and paths
Reading files with cat, less, head and tail
Searching with grep and find
Pipes and redirection
File permissions and ownership with ls -l, chmod and chown
Users, groups and sudo

week_3_4.practice: Solve ten general skills challenges on a practice platform and keep a command notebook

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Windows Administration
topics: Local users and groups, and who should be an administrator
Password and account lockout policies in Local Security Policy
Services: what runs automatically and why that matters
Windows Update, Windows Security and the firewall
Installed programs and how to spot software that should not be there
Event Viewer as a record of what happened
projects: Read-only Windows settings audit on your own computer: users, services and updates checked against a written checklist, nothing changed
week_5_6.practice: Document ten Windows security settings: where each one lives and what the secure value is

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: How Networks Move Data
topics: IP addresses, subnets and the idea of a network
Ports and services: what is listening and why
TCP, UDP and the handshake
DNS and how names become addresses
Reading a packet capture in Wireshark on files we provide
Switches, routers and how traffic finds its way
projects: Packet capture walkthrough: an annotated explanation of a provided capture from first packet to last
week_7_8.practice: Answer a set of questions about two provided packet captures and explain how each answer was found
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a written and practical check on Linux, Windows and networking basics, plus the ethics questions

phase_2_system_hardening.title: PHASE 2: System Hardening in the CyberPatriot Style (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_system_hardening.description: Defence under a clock: securing Windows and Linux systems against a scenario, answering forensics questions, learning network fundamentals and working as a team.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Hardening Windows
topics: Reading the scenario first: which users, software and services are authorised
Removing unauthorised users and fixing administrator rights
Setting password, lockout and audit policies
Disabling unneeded services and features
Updates, firewall and built-in protection settings
Answering forensics questions before changing anything that might destroy evidence
projects: Personal Windows hardening checklist, checked read-only against your own computer's settings
week_9_10.practice: Harden one practice image and record every change made, why it was made and how it was checked

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Hardening Linux
topics: Users, groups and the sudoers file
Password policy and locking unused accounts
Package updates with the system package manager
The uncomplicated firewall, ufw
Securing remote login settings and disabling what is not needed
Finding unwanted software, scheduled tasks and dangerous file permissions
projects: Personal Linux hardening checklist, tested on your own Linux practice virtual machine
week_11_12.practice: Harden one Linux practice image and compare your checklist with a classmate's
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a timed hardening round on a practice image, reviewed item by item against the scenario and your checklist

month_4_networks_and_teamwork.title: Month 4: Network Fundamentals and Team Rounds

topics: IP addressing and subnetting practice
Configuring a small simulated network: addresses, switches and a router
Common server roles and the extra settings they need
Secure file sharing and remote access settings
Networking quiz practice in the style of the Cisco Networking Challenge

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Team Rounds

Splitting work using the scenario and the checklists
Communicating clearly under time pressure
Keeping notes so nothing is done twice or undone
Reviewing a round: what scored, what was missed and why
Competition rules on outside help during a round

phase_3_capture_the_flag.title: PHASE 3: Capture-the-Flag Skills in the picoCTF Style (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_capture_the_flag.description: Puzzle-style security challenges on purpose-built practice platforms: encodings and ciphers, forensics, reading code, and how web and memory bugs are recognised and fixed, ending in a mock CTF.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Encodings and Cryptography
topics: Encodings are not encryption: binary, hexadecimal, ASCII and Base64
Classical ciphers: Caesar, substitution and Vigenere, and how they are broken
XOR and why reusing a key is a mistake
Hashes: what they are for and why passwords are stored as hashes
Public-key encryption explained with small numbers
Writing short Python scripts to automate decoding
projects: Cryptography challenge set solved on a practice platform, with a written solution for each
week_17_18.practice: Solve five cryptography challenges and explain the weakness each one relied on

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Forensics
topics: File signatures and why a file's name can lie about its type
Metadata in images and documents
Hidden data and simple steganography
Searching files and disk images for strings
Packet captures as evidence: following a conversation in Wireshark
Keeping a clean record of what was found and how
projects: Forensics challenge set solved on a practice platform, with a written solution for each
week_19_20.practice: Solve five forensics challenges and write the tool and the clue that cracked each one
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a timed mixed cryptography and forensics set with written solutions

month_6_code_bugs_and_mock_ctf.title: Month 6: Reading Code, Bugs and Fixes, and a Mock CTF

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Reading Code and Recognising Bugs
topics: Reading short Python and C programs to work out what they do
Reverse engineering basics: understanding a program without its source
How web applications trust input, and how input validation fixes that
Injection and cross-site scripting explained with the defender's fix: parameterised queries and output encoding
Memory safety: what a buffer overflow is and how bounds checking prevents it
Practising only on the platform's purpose-built challenges, never on real sites or programs

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Mock CTF and the Road Ahead

week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: mock CTF performance, the hardening and solution portfolio, and a short ethics conversation

faqs.question: Is this course ethical and legal?
faqs.answer: Yes, by design. Students practise only on a practice virtual machine they set up with the teacher and on practice platforms where every challenge is meant to be solved. Every student signs a white-hat agreement in week one: practise only with permission, follow competition rules, and report rather than exploit. When a capture-the-flag challenge involves a bug, students learn the fix a defender would make, not how to use it elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is CyberPatriot?
faqs.answer: CyberPatriot is the National Youth Cyber Education Program created by the Air & Space Forces Association. Its National Youth Cyber Defense Competition puts teams of high school and middle school students in charge of finding and fixing security vulnerabilities in virtual Windows and Linux systems, and teams are scored on how secure they make them. Alongside that Network Security Challenge, CyberPatriot describes a Cisco Networking Challenge made up of an online quiz and a virtual networking exercise. Rounds run online, and teams choose a four-hour period on the competition weekend.

faqs.question: Can you register my teen's CyberPatriot team?
faqs.answer: No. CyberPatriot teams register through a school or approved youth organisation, with an adult coach. A team has between two and six competitors, with up to five competing at a time, in the Open, All Service or Middle School division. This course trains individual students so they bring stronger skills to their team; it is not a team itself. Check eligibility and dates with CyberPatriot directly.

faqs.question: What is picoCTF, and where is it now?
faqs.answer: picoCTF is the capture-the-flag program built by Carnegie Mellon University. picoctf.org now points to CyLab Security Academy, CMU's free cybersecurity learning platform, where existing picoCTF accounts carry over. It has practice challenges across areas such as general skills, cryptography, web exploitation, forensics, binary exploitation and reverse engineering, plus timed events, some of which allow team play.

faqs.question: Does my teen need to know coding?
faqs.answer: No. The first four months are about the command line, system settings and networks rather than programming. Month 5 uses a little Python to automate decoding, and we teach what is needed. Students who already code get more out of the reading-code weeks.

faqs.question: Is this different from your Cybersecurity for Teens course?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cybersecurity for Teens is a broad, defensive introduction to online safety, attacks and defence for any teen, with no coding and no lab setup. This course is hands-on competition preparation: virtual machines, system hardening, network exercises and capture-the-flag practice. Many students take Cybersecurity for Teens first, but it is not required.

faqs.question: What computer does my teen need?
faqs.answer: A laptop or desktop that can run a virtual machine, plus a stable internet connection. Tablets and most Chromebooks are not suitable. We check the computer and help set up the free virtual machine software in the first week.

faqs.question: Will this guarantee a place in a competition final?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody honest can promise that. Results depend on the team, the round and the student's own practice. What the course does is build real skills, tested in timed practice rounds, so a student walks into a competition prepared.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or one to one. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher walks your teen through a short practice challenge, explains the ethics agreement, and suggests whether group, mini batch or one-to-one classes fit best. Parents are welcome to watch. There is no obligation to enrol.
